conventions.convention: Instance, label and action spaces and the predictor class are nonempty; predictors are measurable and the loss is jointly product-measurable with values in [0,+∞]. No IID sampling assumption is implicit.
Samples are ordered and have positive length. Population and empirical risks use extended nonnegative arithmetic and may equal +∞.

If the empirical infimum is +∞, every class member is an exact minimizer. Otherwise an approximate minimizer must have finite risk within a finite tolerance of the infimum. A measurable learning rule requires jointly measurable sample-instance evaluation.

Conditional minimization holds for every action on one measurable full-measure set. AC and standard-Borel instance and label spaces are explicit hypotheses of the conditional Bayes theorem; risks may be infinite.

Under AC, standard-Borel labels suffice for an everywhere conditional probability kernel over an arbitrary nonempty measurable instance space. The proof conditions on the exact uncompleted coordinate sigma-algebra.
Class and unrestricted Bayes risks are distinct infima; attainment is not asserted. Excess risk is defined only when both subtracted terms are finite.
Finite-list selection uses the least eligible index; when all risks are infinite it returns index 1. The tolerance is finite and nonnegative.
Approximate ERM takes an admissible jointly measurable selector as supplied input and asserts no general selector-existence theorem.

load_bearing.statement: A supervised prediction problem consists of nonempty measurable instance, label and action spaces, a probability law on the instance-label product, a nonempty class of measurable predictors, and a product-measurable loss taking values in [0,+∞]; no sample independence or common-law assumption is imposed.

Population risk is the extended nonnegative integral of the predictor's loss under P; empirical risk for an ordered sample of length m≥1 is the average of its m losses. Neither definition assumes finite risk.

In a supervised prediction problem, for every measurable predictor f, the function (x,y)↦ℓ(f(x),y) is measurable, so its population risk is a defined extended nonnegative integral. For every sample size m≥1, the empirical risk S↦R̂_S(f) is an extended nonnegative measurable function on the finite product sample space.

Exact ERM attains the class empirical infimum. Finite-tolerance approximate ERM uses separate finite-infimum and all-infinite branches; a measurable prediction rule has jointly measurable sample-instance evaluation, with no arbitrary-class selector existence asserted.

For a sample of positive length, a finite ordered nonempty list of measurable predictors, and finite tolerance η≥0, the returned index is measurable into the finite discrete index set, its predictor evaluation is jointly measurable, and its output is an η-approximate ERM relative to the list; at η=0 it is exact.

Assume AC. For a joint probability on a nonempty measurable instance space times a nonempty standard-Borel label space, there exists an everywhere probability kernel K with P(C×A)=∫_C K(x,A)P_X(dx). No standard-Borel, countable-generation, or completeness hypothesis is imposed on the instance space.

Assume AC, standard-Borel instance and label spaces, a measurable action space and nonnegative product-measurable loss. A measurable predictor minimizing conditional risk over every action on one measurable full-measure set has population risk no larger than any measurable predictor; all risks may be +∞.

concerns.concern: The Definition includes the correctness assertion 'When η=0, the output is a first exact minimizer, including the all-infinite case' and the work assertion 'The algorithm evaluates only a finite number of empirical risks'. The task requires algorithmic correctness, termination and complexity properties in separate proved results. The existing selector lemma already proves the exact-minimizer assertion; the mathematical procedure itself appears sound.

seams_checked.note: Binary zero-one risks specialize the supplied definitions; IID is added explicitly. Both PAC bounds use the finite-list selector with a finite nonempty class and finite nonnegative tolerance, and retain its measurable exact/approximate ERM guarantees.

Compression permits reconstructed predictors outside the original class, consistent with risk being defined for every measurable predictor. Sample-dependent reconstruction risk measurability is separately justified by joint measurability and Tonelli. PAC-Bayes separately supplies product-measurable bounded loss and parameter-integral measurability.

The consumers use nonnegative population-risk integrals without claiming arbitrary conditional-law or selector existence. A separate finite-label lemma supplies the conditional probability function under AC; the zero-score classification convention is explicitly stated.

Binary bounded risks and finite excess differences match the supplied conventions. The learner's random-risk measurability is expressly required separately, rather than inferred from fixed-predictor empirical-risk measurability.

The algorithm distinguishes empirical and population objectives and expressly requires separate justification for differentiation under expectation; no gradient-unbiasedness consequence is attributed to the risk definitions.

The risk citation is contextual: the particle definition supplies its own Hilbert-space functional R and Bochner-integrability conditions, without claiming that the risk definition proves flow regularity. A separate instance-domain typing omission is reported in alerts.

The reverse-KL theorem explicitly supplies finite discrete feature and label spaces, Borel simplex actions, a singleton measurable predictor class and extended nonnegative cross-entropy. Its proof checks loss measurability and preserves infinite-risk cases.

The pool model specializes to measurable binary predictors and explicitly strengthens distributional zero-risk realizability to a pointwise exact oracle. The remark's finite null-pool witness correctly uses population risk without inferring labels at null instances.

The indistinguishability theorem uses finite discrete joint laws and zero-one loss, so its displayed population risks are exactly the supplier's finite integrals. Common-rule randomization is an explicit finite probability vector.
